newsitem.title: USA: US Dec trade gap bulge hints dollar outlook dimmer.
newsitem.headline: US Dec trade gap bulge hints dollar outlook dimmer.

text.p: A jump in the December U.S. trade deficit reported on Wednesday showed that not all U.S. economic indicators point to an ever-advancing dollar, analysts said.

Since last year, dollar bulls have cited economic fundamentals -- robust U.S. growth, tame inflation and comparatively high interest rates -- like a mantra to explain the steady flow of capital into dollar-based investments.
But they may have ignored the current account, which many analysts consider the number one fundamental factor for the dollar.

As if hypnotized by the dollar's rally in 1996, investors and traders barely blinked as the U.S. racked up record deficits in the quarterly current account, the broadest measure of its international performance, economists said.

The current account -- which includes some investment flows as well as goods and services trade -- has historically been a pivotal component in formulating bets on the long-term path of the dollar. Economists warned that a continually monstrous gap could eventually scare foreigners away from U.S. assets.

"It is certainly true that if we keep running very, very large trade and current account deficits at some point it is going to lead to downward pressure on the dollar," said Robert Hormats, vice chairman at Goldman Sachs (International).

In the last tally, the current account deficit stood at $47.96 billion in the third quarter, up from $40.21 billion in the second and surpassing the previous record shortfall of $43.2 billion set in the fourth quarter of 1987.
Current account data for the final quarter of 1996 is scheduled for release on March 13.
The markets historically tend to ignore data that contradict the prevailing view on the dollar's direction, analysts said.
Currently, market players cite strong U.S. gross domestic product (GDP) growth and bubbling financial markets for whetting investors' appetite for dollars, despite the persistent trade shortfalls.

The U.S. economy whirred along at a 4.7 percent annualized growth rate in the fourth quarter with very low inflation, sucking in capital from overseas. Foreign asset markets can not match such investment returns because higher interest rates would choke off already subpar growth, analysts noted.

As recently as last autumn, smallish monthly trade gaps supported the notion that the rising dollar in 1996 would not cut into U.S. exports. But Wednesday's report on the December trade gap may change that view, economists said.

The U.S. Commerce Department reported the trade deficit in goods and services widened to $10.29 billion in December from an abnormally small $7.94 billion gap in November. The $114.23 billion trade deficit for all of 1996 was the highest since 1988.

"The current account is one of the dollar's key fundamentals and these (trade) figures confirm the view that the current account deficit is widening," said Carl Weinberg, chief economist at High Frequency Economics.
"It means that if capital flows ever hesitate in support of the dollar it will come down," Weinberg added.

As recently as 1995, when the dollar touched record lows versus the yen and mark, foreigners -- reluctant to endorse huge U.S. current account and budget deficits -- shunned dollar investments, particularly U.S. government bonds.
Yet, over the past year the market has mostly ignored the gap because voracious foreign demand for U.S. Treasury securities has compensated for red ink on the trade ledger, economist said.

The dollar rose more than eight percent against the mark and almost 12 percent versus the yen last year. It has continued its surge against those currencies by about 10.5 percent and eight percent respectively so far in 1997, sitting just under multiyear highs set over the past week.
Moreover, Goldman's Hormats noted the U.S. government has pared its budget deficit, reducing the growth of Treasury borrowing over the last two years.
So, to the extent foreigners still soak up U.S. Treasury securities, they free up U.S. capital for more direct investment in the domestic economy, he said.
The growing current account deficit is therefore less an alarm about U.S. over-consumption and its low savings rate than it used to be.
So, the past may not be a perfect guide to the future, economists agreed.

Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities Inc, said while the current account gap may widen, it will not necessarily have a big impact on the dollar and the U.S. bond market over the next one or two quarters.
But experts said if the U.S. economy comes off the boil, or overseas output heats up, allowing foreign interest rates to rise, they are concerned U.S. asset markets could lose their allure.
"That is were the U.S. current account deficit becomes an issue," Iggo said.

"I think the current account deficit is going to come into play at some point," added Bob Lynch, senior currency analyst at MMS International, a market consulting firm. "I can assure you that when the dollar finally does turn down, that will be cited as an issue." ((--212 859 1667)),
